summary: Defines Management Information Bases for running ping, traceroute, and lookup operations from a remote host under network management control. It was later replaced by RFC 4560.

eli5.summary: This lets a manager tell a faraway computer to run network tests like ping and report back.

questions: how to run ping remotely with snmp
subtitle: Use SNMP to remotely trigger ping, traceroute, and DNS lookups on another host and retrieve results.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need to run diagnostic tools like ping and traceroute from remote hosts under management control, but each vendor had their own proprietary MIB. There was no standards-based way to do this.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2925 defines three standardized MIB modules: one for ping (ICMP echo), one for traceroute (path discovery), and one for name lookup (DNS resolution). Each allows a management application to create a test, configure parameters like target address and timeout, and retrieve results including RTT and hop counts.
tldr.outcome: The standard provided a common approach for distributed diagnostics via SNMP. It was later superseded by RFC 4560, which refined the design. The MIBs are widely implemented in network management platforms.

today: RFC 2925 is a Proposed Standard, replaced in 2006 by RFC 4560, which refined the MIBs to address vendor feedback and clarify operational edge cases. The core design—control tables, results tables, and history tables—persists in RFC 4560. Both RFCs are widely implemented in network management platforms.

sections.title: Remote Diagnostics via SNMP
sections.content:
Network management systems need to diagnose connectivity and latency issues from many locations. Traditionally, administrators logged into remote hosts to run tools like ping or traceroute. RFC 2925 standardizes a way to do this via SNMP without logging in: the management station sends an SNMP request asking a remote host to run a test, and the host reports back results including round-trip times, probe responses, and hops traversed.

Before this standard, enterprise MIBs (vendor-specific definitions) filled the gap, but interoperability was poor. RFC 2925 is part of the DISMAN (Distributed Management) working group effort to codify distributed management operations.
sections.eli5: Instead of calling someone and asking them to run ping for you, you tell your network management system to ask them, and it gets the results automatically.

sections.title: Ping Probe Operations
sections.content:
The DISMAN-PING-MIB defines how to initiate and monitor ping tests. A management application creates a row in the pingCtlTable (control table), setting the target address, probe count, timeout, and optionally the implementation method (ICMP echo is recommended; UDP echo, SNMP query, or TCP connection attempt are alternatives).

Once pingCtlAdminStatus is set to enabled, the remote agent begins sending probe packets and records results in the pingResultsTable. This table holds aggregated statistics: minimum, maximum, and average round-trip time (RTT), number of responses, and timestamps. The pingProbeHistoryTable optionally stores per-probe results, with a configurable history size (pingCtlMaxRows).

The ping test can run indefinitely or be scheduled to repeat. Results include response status codes (success, timeout, no route to target, etc.). The agent can send SNMP notifications (traps) when a probe or test fails, or when the test completes.
sections.eli5: You tell the remote computer: send 4 ping packets to 1.2.3.4, wait 5 seconds for each, and ping using ICMP. It does that and tells you how many came back and how long they took.

sections.title: Traceroute Path Discovery
sections.content:
The DISMAN-TRACEROUTE-MIB allows discovery of the hops along a path to a destination. It mirrors the ping MIB structure: a traceRouteCtlTable configures the test, a traceRouteResultsTable holds aggregated results, and a traceRouteProbeHistoryTable stores per-probe details.

Unlike ping, traceroute must increase the IP time-to-live (TTL) in successive probes to discover intermediate hops. Parameters include traceRouteCtlMaxTtl (maximum TTL value, typically 30) and traceRouteCtlProbesPerHop (number of probes per hop, often 3). The agent uses UDP probes to an unlikely port (recommended) or ICMP echo, and processes ICMP time-exceeded messages to identify each hop.

Results are stored in the traceRouteHopsTable, with one entry per hop found, including the hop address and round-trip times. The agent can abort if too many consecutive hops fail (controlled by traceRouteCtlMaxFailures), since a traceroute to an unreachable host would otherwise take hours.
sections.eli5: You ask the remote host: show me every hop between here and 1.2.3.4. It sends probes with increasing TTL values, collects the hop addresses and response times, and reports back.

sections.title: DNS Lookup and Reverse Lookup
sections.content:
The DISMAN-NSLOOKUP-MIB enables remote name resolution: forward lookup (hostname to IP address) and reverse lookup (IP address to hostname). A management application creates a row in the lookupCtlTable with a target name or address.

When lookupCtlTargetAddressType is set to dns, the agent performs gethostbyname() to resolve the name to addresses. When set to ipv4 or ipv6, it performs gethostbyaddr() to resolve the address to names. Results are stored in the lookupResultsTable, which can hold multiple entries per lookup (since a hostname may resolve to many addresses, and an address may have multiple DNS names).

This operation is useful for discovering the symbolic names of hops discovered by traceroute without needing another round-trip to the management station.
sections.eli5: You ask the remote host: what is the IP address of example.com? Or: what is the hostname for 1.2.3.4? It looks it up and tells you.

sections.title: Concurrency, Timing, and Notifications
sections.content:
Each MIB module defines a MaxConcurrentRequests object that limits how many simultaneous tests an agent can run. This prevents resource exhaustion. Default limits vary but are often small (e.g., 4 concurrent pings).

Timing parameters control test duration. A ping test with default timeout (5 seconds) and probe count (3) takes at most 15 seconds, plus network latency. A traceroute with defaults can take 4.5 minutes (30 hops times 3 probes times 5-second timeout). Administrators can set longer timeouts and probe counts if needed, accepting longer test times.

When tests fail or complete, the agent can generate SNMP notifications: pingProbeFailed, pingTestFailed, and pingTestCompleted. This allows management applications to react in real-time without polling results. The lookup MIB includes a lookupPurgeTime object to automatically delete completed lookup entries after a set interval.
sections.eli5: The remote host can run a few tests at once but not unlimited. Tests take time based on how many probes you ask for and how long you wait for answers. You can ask to be notified when tests finish instead of polling.

sections.title: Security and Administrative Control
sections.content:
Each MIB entry is indexed by SnmpAdminString, allowing SNMP access controls (VACM, View-Based Access Control Model, from RFC 2575) to segregate test ownership. Different administrators can create and manage their own tests without interfering with others.

The RFC notes that ping and traceroute can be abused: excessive probing can degrade target performance, and attempting connections to unknown ports can trigger alerts. Implementations SHOULD rate-limit or throttle operations. Access controls MUST be configured to prevent unauthorized users from initiating tests.

Note that some routers and hosts rate-limit or drop ICMP entirely, or do not respond to ICMP echo requests addressed to network addresses. This can cause false negatives in ping tests. The RFC recommends UDP probes for traceroute rather than ICMP, since some networks filter ICMP Echo Requests but permit UDP to unused ports.
sections.eli5: Only authorized people should be able to ask the remote host to run tests. Running too many tests too fast might disrupt the target host. Firewalls might block probes, giving wrong answers.

left.title: Before RFC 2925
left.desc: Each vendor has its own proprietary MIB; no interoperability.

right.title: After RFC 2925
right.desc: Standard DISMAN MIBs; any SNMP manager can interoperate.
